{{Short description|Model for topological superconductors in physics}}
In [[condensed matter physics]], the '''Kitaev chain''' or '''Kitaev–Majorana chain''' is a simplified model for a [[topological superconductor]]. It models a one dimensional lattice featuring [[Majorana fermion#Majorana bound states|Majorana bound states]]. The Kitaev chain has been used as a [[toy model]] of semiconductor nanowires for the development of [[topological quantum computer]]s.<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Wright |first=Katherine |date=2023-02-15 |title=Evidence Found for a Majorana "Cousin" |url=https://physics.aps.org/articles/v16/24#c1 |journal=Physics |language=en |volume=16 |article-number=24|doi=10.1103/Physics.16.24 |bibcode=2023PhyOJ..16...24W }}</ref><ref name=":2">{{Cite web |date=2024 |title='Poor man's Majoranas' offer testbed for studying possible qubits |url=https://physicsworld.com/a/poor-mans-majoranas-offer-testbed-for-studying-possible-qubits/ |access-date=2024-09-10 |website=Physics World |language=en-GB}}</ref> The model was first proposed by [[Alexei Kitaev]] in 2000.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kitaev |first=A Yu |date=2001-10-01 |title=Unpaired Majorana fermions in quantum wires |url=https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1070/1063-7869/44/10S/S29 |journal=Physics-Uspekhi |volume=44 |issue=10S |pages=131–136 |doi=10.1070/1063-7869/44/10S/S29 |issn=1468-4780|arxiv=cond-mat/0010440 }}</ref>

== Description ==

=== Hamiltonian ===
The [[tight binding]] [[Hamiltonian (quantum mechanics)|Hamiltonian]] of a Kitaev chain considers a one dimensional lattice with ''N'' site and spinless particles at zero temperature, subjected to nearest neighbour hopping interactions, given in [[second quantization]] formalism as<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Schäpers |first=Thomas |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=vdIuEAAAQBAJ&dq=kitaev+chain&pg=PA349 |title=Semiconductor Spintronics |date=2021-05-10 |publisher=Walter de Gruyter GmbH & Co KG |isbn=978-3-11-063900-1 |language=en}}</ref>
:<math>H=-\mu\sum_{j=1}^N \left(c_j^\dagger c_j-\frac12\right)+\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\left[-t\left(c_{j+1}^\dagger c_j+c_j^\dagger c_{j+1}\right)+|\Delta|\left(c_{j+1}^\dagger c_j^\dagger+c_j c_{j+1}\right)\right]</math>
There<math>\mu </math> is the [[chemical potential]], <math>c_j^\dagger,c_j</math> are [[creation and annihilation operators]], <math>t\geq 0</math> the energy needed for a particle to hop from one location of the lattice to another, <math>\Delta=|\Delta|e^{i\theta}</math> is the induced superconducting gap (p-wave pairing) and <math>\theta</math> is the coherent superconducting phase. This Hamiltonian has particle-hole symmetry, as well as [[time reversal symmetry]].<ref name=":3">{{Cite book |last=Stanescu |first=Tudor D. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=gg4GEQAAQBAJ |title=Introduction to Topological Quantum Matter & Quantum Computation |date=2024-07-02 |publisher=CRC Press |isbn=978-1-040-04198-7 |language=en}}</ref>

The Hamiltonian can be rewritten using Majorana operators, given by<ref name=":0" />
:<math>\left\{
\begin{matrix}
\gamma^{\rm A}_j=c_j^\dagger+c_j\\ \gamma^{\rm B}_j=i(c_j^\dagger-c_j)
\end{matrix}
\right.
</math>,
which can be thought as the real and imaginary parts of the annihilation operator <math>c_j=\tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma^{\rm A}_j+i\gamma^{\rm B}_j)
</math>.  These Majorana operators are [[Hermitian operator]]s, and [[Anticommutator|anticommutate]],
:<math>\{\gamma^\alpha_j,\gamma^\beta_k\}=2 \delta_{jk}\delta_{\alpha \beta}
</math>.
Using these operators the Hamiltonian can be rewritten as<ref name=":0" />
:<math>H=-\frac{i\mu}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N \gamma^{\rm B}_j \gamma^{\rm A}_j+\frac{i}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\left(\omega_+\gamma^{\rm B}_j\gamma^{\rm A}_{j+1}+\omega_-\gamma^{\rm B}_{j+1}\gamma^{\rm A}_j\right)</math>
where <math>\omega_\pm=|\Delta|\pm t</math>.

=== Trivial phase ===
In the limit <math>t=|\Delta|\to 0</math>, we obtain the following Hamiltonian
:<math>H=-\frac{i\mu}{2}\sum_{j=1}^N \gamma^{\rm B}_j \gamma^{\rm A}_j</math>
where the Majorana operators are coupled on the same site. This condition is considered a topologically trivial phase.<ref name=":3" />

=== Non-trivial phase ===
In the limit <math>\mu\to 0</math> and <math>|\Delta|\to t</math>, we obtain the following Hamiltonian
:<math>H_{\rm M}=it\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\gamma^{\rm B}_j\gamma^{\rm A}_{j+1}</math>
where every Majorana operator is coupled to a Majorana operator of a different kind in the next site. By assigning a new fermion operator <math>\tilde{c}_j=\tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma^{\rm B}_j+i\gamma^{\rm A}_{j+1})
</math>, the Hamiltonian is diagonalized, as
:<math>H_{\rm M}=2t\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\left(\tilde{c}^\dagger_j \tilde{c}_j+\frac{1}{2}\right)</math>
which describes a new set of ''N''-1 [[Bogoliubov quasiparticle]]s with energy ''t''. The missing mode given by  <math>\tilde{c}_{\rm M}=\tfrac{1}{2}(\gamma^{\rm B}_N+i\gamma^{\rm A}_{1})
</math> couples the Majorana operators from the two endpoints of the chain, as this mode does not appear in the Hamiltonian, it requires zero energy. This mode is called a Majorana zero mode and is highly delocalized. As the presence of this mode does not change the total energy, the ground state is two-fold degenerate.<ref name=":0" /> This condition is a topological superconducting non-trivial phase.<ref name=":3" />

The existence of the Majorana zero mode is [[Symmetry-protected topological order|topologically protected from small perturbation due to symmetry considerations]]. For the Kitaev chain the Majorana zero mode persist as long as <math>\mu<2t</math> and the superconducting gap is finite.<ref name=":7">{{Cite web |last=Topology course team |date=2021 |title=Bulk-edge correspondence in the Kitaev chain |url=https://topocondmat.org/w1_topointro/1D.html |website=Online course on topology in condensed matter - Delft University of Technology}}</ref> The robustness of these modes makes it a candidate for [[qubit]]s as a basis for [[topological quantum computer]].<ref name=":6">{{Cite web |last=Ball |first=Philip |date=2021-09-29 |title=Major Quantum Computing Strategy Suffers Serious Setbacks |url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/major-quantum-computing-strategy-suffers-serious-setbacks-20210929/ |access-date=2024-09-10 |website=Quanta Magazine |language=en}}</ref>

== Bulk case ==
Using Bogoliubov-de Gennes formalism it can be shown that for the bulk case (infinite number of sites), that the energy yields<ref name=":7" />
:<math>E(k)=\pm\sqrt{(2t\cos k+\mu)^2+4|\Delta|^2\sin^2k}</math>,
and it is gapped, except for the case <math>\mu=2t</math> and wave vector <math>k=0</math>. For the bulk case there are no zero modes. However a [[topological invariant]] exists given by 
:<math>Q=\mathrm{sign}\left\{\mathrm{pf}[iH(k=0)]\mathrm{pf}[iH(k=\pi)]\right\}</math>,
where <math>\mathrm{pf}[x]</math> is the [[Pfaffian]] operation. For <math>\mu>2t</math>, the invariant is strictly <math>Q=1</math> and for <math>\mu<2t</math>, <math>Q=-1</math> corresponding to the trivial and non-trivial phases from the finite chain, respectively. This relation between the topological invariant from the bulk case and the existence of Majorana zero modes in the finite case is called a bulk-edge correspondence.<ref name=":7" />

== Experimental efforts ==
One possible realization of Kitaev chains is using semiconductor nanowires with strong [[spin–orbit interaction]] to break spin-degeneracy,<ref name=":4">{{Cite web |last=Topology course team |date=2021 |title=From Kitaev chain to a nanowire |url=https://topocondmat.org/w2_majorana/nanowire.html |website=Online course on topology in condensed matter – University of Delft}}</ref> like [[indium antimonide]] or [[indium arsenide]].<ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Fei |last2=Matern |first2=Stephanie |date=2014 |title=Kitaev Chain |url=https://www.thp.uni-koeln.de/trebst/Lectures/Seminar14/Handout8.pdf |journal=Oberseminar: Quantum Knots - Prof. Dr A. Rosch, Prof. Dr. S. Trebst - University of Cologne}}</ref> A magnetic field can be applied to induce [[Zeeman effect|Zeeman coupling]] to spin polarize the wire and break [[Kramers degeneracy]].<ref name=":4" /> The superconducting gap can be induced using [[Andreev reflection]], by putting the wire in the proximity to a superconductor.<ref name=":4" /><ref name=":5" /> Realizations using 3D topological insulators have also been proposed.<ref name=":5" />

There is no single definitive way to test for Majorana zero modes. One proposal to experimentally observe these modes is using [[Scanning tunneling microscope|scanning tunneling microscopy]].<ref name=":5" /> A zero bias peak in the conductance could be the signature of a topological phase.<ref name=":5" /> [[Josephson effect]] between two wires in superconducting phase could also help to demonstrate these modes.<ref name=":5" />

In 2023 QuTech team from [[Delft University of Technology]] reported the realization of a poor man's Majorana, a Kitaev chain with two or three sites that produces a Majorana bound state that is not [[Symmetry-protected topological order|topologically protected]] and therefore only stable for a very small range of parameters.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> It was obtained in a Kitaev chain consisting of two [[quantum dot]]s in a superconducting [[nanowire]] strongly coupled by normal [[Quantum tunnelling|tunneling]] and [[Andreev tunneling]] with the state arising when the rate of both processes match.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /> Some researches have raised concerns, suggesting that an alternative mechanism to that of Majorana bound states might explain the data obtained.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":6" />

In 2024, the first experiment in an optomechanical network was conducted to create a [[Boson|bosonic]] analogue of a Kitaev chain.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Slim |first1=Jesse J. |last2=Wanjura |first2=Clara C. |last3=Brunelli |first3=Matteo |last4=del Pino |first4=Javier |last5=Nunnenkamp |first5=Andreas |last6=Verhagen |first6=Ewold |date=2024-03-28 |title=Optomechanical realization of the bosonic Kitaev chain |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07174-w |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=627 |issue=8005 |pages=767–771 |doi=10.1038/s41586-024-07174-w |pmid=38538943 |issn=0028-0836|arxiv=2309.05825 |bibcode=2024Natur.627..767S }}</ref>
